
  Not checked: why rclone fails (probably an expired OneDrive token), and how much space the new setting saves once targets rebuild. The commit skipped the pre-commit hook because pre-commit wasn't on PATH.

✻ Cogitated for 36s · done 12:02

❯ back to optimization: 7G that you said needs btrfs, - can you tell me comparison in the cocmpilation speed on btrfs vs ext4 in the first place. Cause I think ext4 is faster to compile on no? So we'd be looking at a pros/cons table

  // spawn an agent to use chrome through debug port and solve the expired one drive token (or wait, do we even have anything using it, - mb we can turn it off for now)

  Thought for 35s, ran 2 shell commands

● Agent(Reconnect rclone OneDrive token) Sonnet 5
  ⎿  Backgrounded agent (↓ to manage · ctrl+o to expand)

  Thought for 10s

● I started an agent to reconnect the OneDrive token in your Chrome. Nothing in your code or repos uses OneDrive; you added the mount on 09-17 as a plain folder. The token is empty, and rclone says so. If the agent hits a password or 2FA
  prompt, the fallback is to disable the service.

  ext4 vs btrfs for compiling. Yes, ext4 is faster, but by little: compiling is mostly CPU, not disk. This comes from what I remember of Phoronix-style benchmarks, not a measurement on your machine:

                        ext4            btrfs                    XFS
   compile speed        baseline        ~0–10% slower            ≈ ext4
                                        (CoW + checksums on
                                        many small writes)
   dedup of shared deps ✗               ✓ but offline only       ✓ offline only
                                        (bees / duperemove;      (duperemove)
                                        sccache & cargo write
                                        fresh files, not reflinks)
   transparent zstd     ✗               ✓ compress=zstd:1        ✗
   snapshots            ✗               ✓                        ✗
   migration cost       —               reformat / btrfs-convert reformat

  btrfs's real win for target/ is compression, not dedup. Debug info and rlibs compress about 2–3×. That beats the ~7G dedup ceiling, and it already covers your 18G of binaries. The cost is a little CPU on every write.

  I'd stay on ext4 for now: after line-tables-only and with cargo sweep on a cron, measure target/ again. Most of the 39G was debug info, so the case for reformatting your root fs will probably go away. If it doesn't, the cheapest step is a
  separate btrfs partition with compress=zstd for CARGO_TARGET_DIR/sccache only, not converting root.

  I haven't benchmarked this on your hardware. Hardlink-dedup tools like jdupes -L on ext4 aren't safe for build outputs, and I haven't checked whether cargo ever writes those files in place.
